newsitem.title: FRANCE: Credit Lyonnais in black, wants more state cash.
newsitem.headline: Credit Lyonnais in black, wants more state cash.

text.p: State-owned bank Credit Lyonnais reported a modest first-half profit of 67 million francs ($12.9 million) on Thursday, helped by a big dose of public money, and warned it would need further cash before it could be privatised.
The bank, still digging out from an expansion spree in the late 1980s that nearly bankrupted it, had a first half profit of 36 million francs last year.
It was spared the humiliation of a return to the red by a 3.9 billion franc state emergency aid package announced last week.
The aid was aimed at removing the burden of most of the costs imposed on the bank as part of a state bailout last year. Without it, a loss of at least two billion francs was expected.
The government said last week the state aid was a prelude to another rescue for the bank, the third in three years, to ready it for a fast sale. It had planned to sell it in the year 2000.

Bank chairman Jean Peyrelevade said it would need more state money to boost its balance sheet to be privatised. "If people want a rapid (privatisation), it would need a recapitalisation (by the state)," he said.

He said the bank's 4.5 percent Cooke ratio -- an international standard to measure bank solvency -- was inadequate to attract buyers. He estimated that to raise it by one percentage point would take seven to eight billion francs.
"None of our partners --- French or European -- would accept the risk of a deterioration of its own rating by taking a minority or majority stake in Lyonnais (now)," he said.

He welcomed the planned sale and promised a plan by the end of the year to prpeare the bank for privatisation. But he warned the sell-off would take time and a source close to the bank said it was not expected to take place until at least early 1998.
The results were delayed by a week to give the state time to win the European Commission's approval for the emergency aid.

The Commission, which reluctantly cleared last year's 45 billion franc rescue, is expected to impose stringent new conditions, including a demand for more asset disposals, in exchange for approving another bail-out.
But an official close to the bank said the Commission could not be too tough as its own rules stipulated that it had to "ensure the viability of the enterprise."
Peyrelevade said the bank would need to make more disposals to be privatised as it was too big but would not give up strategic assets. He would not say which ones were strategic.

Net banking income -- the banking equivalent of turnover -- fell to 21.5 billion francs from 22.1 billion. But on a like-for-like basis, it rose 3.9 percent. Net operating profit rose 20.1 percent to 4.2 billion francs.
"I said last year Credit Lyonnais was walking again on its two feet," Peyrelevade said. The results "confirm this."
He was modest, however, in his full year profit target, saying he would be satisfied if the bank broke even.
The profit was after a 35 million franc payment to the state under a clause in last year's bailout that dictated that it must pay a third of its earnings into public coffers until 2014.
Net operating provisions fell to 2.3 billion francs from 2.5 billion. The bank also made a 1.3 billion provision to cover its restructuring under which it will cut 5,000 jobs by end 1998.

All four of its activity areas were in profit for the first time since 1993. But results worsened in France, where margins remained under pressure in a fiercely competitive banking climate. But in Europe overall, the situation improved with like-for-like operating income up 23 percent.
The bank rocketed in size during the late 1980s, then came crashing down to earth in the early 1990s when property values collapsed and European economic growth evaporated.
The bank eked out a 13 million franc profit for 1995 after racking up losses of 21 billion francs between 1992 and 1994.
The ultimate bill to taxpayers for keeping the bank alive is expected to hit at least 100 billion francs with some analysts estimating it could run as high as 125 billion or more.
